title: A sky photo is expected to appear in Memories
preconditions: A adds a photo in Us.
B expects every shared photo to appear in Memories.
Neither has read the explanation of the two destinations.

actions.note: A chooses a photo for the sky.
B searches Memories for the same photo.

expected_behavior: The app makes clear that a sky photo and a dated memory are separate actions.
A sky photo does not silently become a dated memory.
The archive remains the complete place to browse dated content.
candidate_failure_modes: B concludes the photo failed to save.
A believes one action published to both destinations.
The app adds a second, unrequested copy to resolve the ambiguity.

observed_code_behavior: Us and Memories are intentionally separate destinations; sky photos are not dated memories.
Free and Plus see the same relationship home.

hypothetical_user_behavior: A fictional participant (Vera Lind) said: "We are auditing Aoi for things that do not need to exist. Walk through Us and Memories as you actually used them: the photo sky, the history control, the help panel, the add-photo action, the dated-memory action, the distinction between the two surfaces, and every label or decoration around them. For each one, ask out loud: "Why does this even exist?" Then say what would break if it were removed, and what it cost you. Name the three most useless things and the one thing you would keep. Do not propose a redesign; remove."

A fictional participant (Wolf Adler) said: "Ran it exactly as asked, on the surfaces as I actually used them, not as they're described.

"WHY DOES THIS EVEN EXIST?" — three answers:

1) The photo sky. Removing it breaks nothing: every photo in it is reachable from the memory list, in the same order, with the same captions. It cost me a hijacked scroll and, twice, a back gesture that took me out of the surface when I was trying to leave the sky. That is the worst possible trade: zero information gained, a navigation exit risk paid.

2) The dated-memory action. It writes a date onto a row that already prints that date. Removing it removes one tap and one duplicate label and loses no capability. It exists, as far as I can tell, because something else needed a button-shaped thing next to it.

3) The help panel. This one is the interesting one. It restates the labels it sits beside — so as help, it's decoration. But it is also the only place in the entire product that admits the add-photo action can fail. That is not help, that's a confession in a drawer. Removing the panel is correct only once that sentence is moved to where the failure actually happens; moving the sentence is not a redesign, it's putting copy where the event is.

THE ONE I WOULD KEEP: the history control. It is the only affordance that let me get back out of an edit without losing the draft. Every other back route in Us and Memories exits mid-edit. Keep it, and keep it doing exactly that.

The distinction between the two surfaces, for the record: Us is where things happen; Memories is where things are listed. Almost everything useless above is Us pretending to be Memories.

EXACT REPRODUCTION — silent add-photo failure (patchy connection, switch access):
1. Us → add-photo → choose a photo.
2. Spinner appears. It is not a status; it has no text, no progress, no cancel.
3. At ~6s the surface returns to itself. No error. No toast. Draft gone.
4. The label on the action still reads as though it succeeded.
Expected: a message that says it failed, and the draft still there. Actual: a spinner that means nothing and a label that means the opposite of what happened.

A spinner is not a status. A code field that won't accept a pasted message is the same bug wearing a different coat."
Vera Lind assumes: the app should never make me guess
Vera Lind assumes: a failed action must preserve my input
Wolf Adler assumes: a spinner is not a status
Wolf Adler assumes: a code field should accept a pasted message
